lesson.title: Making Something New: Chemical Changes and Chemical Reactions
lesson.summary: This section defines chemical change as the formation of new substances through bond rearrangement, with the combustion of methane as a fully balanced worked example.
lesson.body:
The chemical properties discussed earlier in this unit describe how a substance can react, and a chemical change is what happens when that potential is actually realized: atoms rearrange their bonds so that one or more entirely new substances form, each with its own distinct set of physical and chemical properties different from what you started with. This is the sharp line between a chemical change and the physical changes covered in the previous section. Melting ice still leaves you with H2O; burning a piece of wood does not leave you with wood in a different shape, it leaves you with ash, carbon dioxide gas, and water vapor, substances with chemical formulas, densities, colors, and reactivities completely unlike the wood's original cellulose.

Because a chemical change is not always as visually obvious as combustion, chemists rely on several telltale signs, though none of them proves a chemical change occurred on its own. A color change that cannot be explained by simple mixing, the production of gas bubbles from two liquids that were not fizzy before, the formation of a solid precipitate when two clear solutions are combined, an unexpected release or absorption of heat, and the emission of light are all common evidence that bonds have broken and reformed into new substances. When a solution of silver nitrate is combined with a solution of sodium chloride, a white solid, silver chloride, instantly precipitates out of the clear liquid: AgNO3 (aq) plus NaCl (aq) yields AgCl (s) plus NaNO3 (aq). The clear, colorless silver nitrate and clear, colorless sodium chloride solutions did not simply mix; their ions rearranged into a genuinely new solid compound.

Combustion is one of the most familiar chemical changes, and the burning of natural gas offers a clean worked example. Methane, CH4, reacts with oxygen gas according to the balanced equation CH4 + 2O2 to CO2 + 2H2O. One methane molecule combines with two oxygen molecules to produce one carbon dioxide molecule and two water molecules, releasing a substantial amount of heat and light in the process, which is why methane is burned as a fuel. Notice that the equation is balanced: four hydrogen atoms appear on both sides, four oxygen atoms appear on both sides, two from CO2 and two from the pair of H2O molecules, and one carbon atom appears on both sides. This balancing reflects conservation of mass, the same principle from the physical changes section: no atoms vanish or appear from nowhere during the reaction, they are only rearranged into new molecular partners, so the total mass of CH4 and O2 consumed exactly equals the total mass of CO2 and H2O produced.

Chemical changes are, in a real sense, the central subject of chemistry as a discipline, since nearly everything chemists study, from digesting food to manufacturing pharmaceuticals to generating energy in a battery, involves substances transforming into other substances through the breaking and forming of chemical bonds. Recognizing the difference between a physical change, which alters appearance or state without touching chemical identity, and a chemical change, which produces genuinely new substances, is one of the most fundamental skills this unit builds, and it is a skill that every later topic in this course, from stoichiometry to equilibrium to thermodynamics, assumes you already have solid.
